title: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
summary: How AD, NTLM and Kerberos work, and how attackers abuse them: relay, Kerberoasting, delegation, forged tickets, DCSync, ACL paths and AD CS, with the logs, fixes and tiering that stop them.
outcomes: Explain how domains, forests, trusts, DCs, LDAP, OUs and GPOs fit together and why privileged groups are the target
Trace NTLM and Kerberos message by message and explain why a hash or a service key works as a password
Explain Kerberoasting, AS-REP roasting, delegation abuse, golden and silver tickets and DCSync, and detect each in DC logs
Audit a domain with read-only PowerShell for SPNs, pre-auth, delegation, replication rights, ACLs and AD CS templates
Write detections for key events (4768, 4769, 4771, 4776, 4662, 4742) and a Sigma rule for Kerberoasting
Apply tiering, Protected Users, LAPS and gMSAs, and plan recovery after a domain compromise

lessons.title: What Active Directory is: one directory for thousands of machines

blocks.md:
The Windows course ended with a first look at domains: instead of every laptop keeping its own accounts, computers **join a domain** and ask a central directory who people are. This lesson opens that directory up, because every attack in this course abuses one part of it.

Tiny example: Contoso has 3,000 employees, 3,200 laptops and 400 servers. Ana joins on Monday. An admin creates **one** account for Ana, adds it to two groups, and by lunchtime Ana can sign in to any laptop, open the finance share and read email. Nobody touched the 3,600 machines. Every one of them asked the directory.

A **directory** is a hierarchical store of information about objects on a network; a **directory service** stores that data and makes it findable. **Active Directory Domain Services** (AD DS, usually just AD, Microsoft's directory service) stores user accounts, computer accounts, groups, printers and servers, plus the rules for finding and securing them.

The pieces you will meet in every lesson:
- **Domain**: a boundary of administration and replication, named like a DNS name (`contoso.com`). It has its own accounts and its own Domain Admins group.
- **Domain controller (DC)**: a server that holds a full, writable copy of the domain's directory and answers sign-in requests (a read-only DC, RODC, keeps a read-only copy for branch offices). Every DC in a domain replicates every change to the others.
- **Directory database**: on each DC the data lives in a file, `ntds.dit` under `%windir%\Ntds` by default.
- **Schema**: the rules that define which object classes and attributes may exist.

- **Forest**: one or more domains that share a schema, a configuration and a **global catalog** (an index of every object in the forest). Domains can form **trees**, a parent and its children such as `contoso.com` and `eu.contoso.com`.
- **Trust**: a relationship that lets accounts from one domain be authenticated in another. Every domain inside an on-premises forest trusts the others through automatic two-way **transitive** trusts (if A trusts B and B trusts C, A trusts C). Separate forests can be linked by a **forest trust**.
- **LDAP** (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol, the Internet standard for reading and writing directories modelled on the X.500 directory standards): how programs query AD, on TCP port 389.
- **OU** (organizational unit): a folder-like container inside a domain. OUs exist to delegate administration and to target policy.
- **GPO** (Group Policy Object): a bundle of settings stored in AD and linked to a site, a domain or an OU; machines and users under that link apply it at startup and sign-in.

blocks.title: One forest, two domains, and where the pieces live

scenes.caption: A forest holds one or more domains. The first domain is the forest root; eu.contoso.com was added as a child and got an automatic two-way transitive trust.
Each domain has domain controllers. Each DC keeps a full copy of its domain's directory in ntds.dit, and changes replicate to every DC in the domain.
Inside the domain, OUs group objects. A GPO linked to the Finance laptops OU configures every computer placed there.
Ana's laptop talks to a DC: LDAP to look things up, Kerberos to sign in. Whoever controls the DCs controls every answer the laptop gets.

blocks.md:
Why attackers care: AD is the one place that decides **who is who** and **who may do what** for thousands of machines. Control a DC, or anything that can write to the directory, and you control everyone who trusts it. Defenders call the DCs and everything that can control them **Tier 0** (lesson 14).

The directory is also readable. By design, any authenticated domain user can query most of it over LDAP, because laptops need to look up users, groups and services. That is convenient for applications and for attackers doing **reconnaissance** (mapping the target), and it is just as useful to you: everything below can be audited from a normal admin workstation with read-only queries.

blocks.code:
# Read-only: describe the forest and domain you are in (RSAT ActiveDirectory module)
Import-Module ActiveDirectory

Get-ADForest | Select-Object Name, RootDomain, Domains, GlobalCatalogs
Get-ADDomain | Select-Object DNSRoot, NetBIOSName, DomainMode, PDCEmulator
Get-ADDomainController -Filter * | Select-Object HostName, Site, IsGlobalCatalog, OperatingSystem

# Trusts this domain has with other domains or forests
Get-ADTrust -Filter * | Select-Object Name, Direction, ForestTransitive

# OUs and the GPOs linked to each one
Get-ADOrganizationalUnit -Filter * -Properties gPLink | Select-Object DistinguishedName, gPLink
blocks.caption: Audit queries a defender runs first. The ActiveDirectory module ships with RSAT (Remote Server Administration Tools).

blocks.md: A domain is not a wall. Domains in one forest trust each other automatically, and the Enterprise Admins group of the forest root is an administrator in every domain (next lesson). Plan protection for the whole forest, not one domain at a time.

AD is a replicated database of identities and rules. DCs hold it, LDAP reads it, Kerberos and NTLM use it to sign people in, and GPOs push its settings to machines. Every attack in this course either steals proof of an identity or gains the right to write to this database.

blocks.question: An attacker has a normal domain user account and no admin rights anywhere. What can they usually do with LDAP?
options: Read most of the directory: users, groups, computers, SPNs and many attributes
Nothing: LDAP requires Domain Admin rights
Write any attribute of any object
Only read their own account
blocks.explain: Most of AD is readable by any authenticated user because clients need it. That is why reconnaissance needs no privileges, and why defenders should run the same queries first.

blocks.question: Contoso links a GPO that turns on detailed audit logging to the OU 'Finance laptops'. Ana's laptop sits in the OU 'Sales laptops'. Does Ana's laptop get the setting?
options: Yes, every GPO applies to every machine in the forest
Only after the DC restarts
No, unless the same GPO is also linked at the domain, the site or an OU above Sales laptops
Yes, because Ana is in the Finance group
blocks.explain: Computer settings apply by where the computer object sits: its site, its domain and its OU chain. Group membership of the user does not move the computer into Finance.

lessons.title: Privileged groups, and why so many paths lead to Domain Admins

blocks.md:
Microsoft's own guidance names three built-in groups as the most powerful in AD, plus a fourth:
- **Enterprise Admins** (EA): lives only in the forest root domain and can make forest-wide changes, such as adding domains or creating forest trusts. By default it is a member of the built-in Administrators group of **every** domain in the forest.
- **Domain Admins** (DA): one per domain, RID 512 (recall SIDs from the Windows course). It is a member of its domain's Administrators group and of the local Administrators group on **every** domain-joined computer.
- **Administrators** (built-in, BA): the group that actually holds most rights on directory objects and on the DCs.
- **Schema Admins**: can change the schema, the rules for the whole forest.

Tiny example: Ana is added to Domain Admins to fix one printer queue. Ana's account is now an administrator of all 3,600 machines, including every DC.

Below them sit the **operator groups**, built in for delegation: **Account Operators** (administer users and groups), **Backup Operators** (may bypass file security to back up or restore), **Server Operators** and **Print Operators**. They look modest, but Backup Operators, for example, may sign in locally to DCs and back up any file regardless of its permissions, so attackers treat these groups as stepping stones.

**Why paths converge.** Groups **nest**: if group A is a member of group B, every member of A gets B's rights. Nesting is invisible in a quick glance at a group, so an account can be a Domain Admin through three levels of groups nobody remembers creating. Add machines where admins have signed in (their credentials sit in LSASS memory, recall the Windows course) and objects whose permissions let one user change another, and you get many routes that all end at DA. Lesson 11 turns those routes into a graph.

blocks.title: Nesting: how Ben becomes an admin of every machine

scenes.caption: Ben is in Helpdesk-L2. On its own that group has no special rights.
Years ago someone nested Helpdesk-L2 inside IT-Server-Ops to save time.
And IT-Server-Ops was nested in Domain Admins. Ben is now effectively a Domain Admin, and no single group page shows it.
Domain Admins sits in the domain's Administrators group and every computer's local Administrators group. Ben's phished laptop is now a path to the whole domain.

blocks.md:
**AdminSDHolder.** Because people with delegated rights could otherwise grant themselves control over admin accounts, AD protects a fixed list of accounts and groups (Administrators, Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, Schema Admins, the operator groups, krbtgt and others). A process called **SDProp** runs every 60 minutes by default on the DC holding the PDC emulator role (one DC per domain that plays the part of the old Windows NT primary domain controller, PDC) and resets the permissions on those protected objects to match a template object, `CN=AdminSDHolder,CN=System` in the domain. The flip side: anyone who can edit the AdminSDHolder object can plant a permission that SDProp copies onto every admin account each hour, so its permissions deserve the same monitoring as Domain Admins membership.

**Detection.** Additions to security groups are logged on DCs: for example event **4732** for a member added to a security-enabled local group such as Administrators, and **4728** for a global group such as Domain Admins. Alert on any change to the privileged groups and to AdminSDHolder.

blocks.caption: Read-only. Run it monthly and diff the output: every name should have a ticket explaining why it is there.

blocks.prompt: Microsoft recommends that Domain Admins membership be needed only in 'break glass' situations. Contoso has 41 Domain Admins, most of whom sign in to their own laptops with those accounts every day. Before reading on, how many machines does an attacker need to compromise to get Domain Admin?
blocks.reveal:
Potentially just **one**: any laptop where one of those 41 accounts has signed in interactively. With local admin there, the attacker can read the cached credential material from LSASS (Windows course, lesson 8) and replay it.

That is why the fix is not only fewer admins but **separate accounts**: Ana's daily account reads email; Ana's admin account signs in only to admin systems. Lesson 14 formalises this as tiering.

blocks.md: Enterprise Admins, Domain Admins and built-in Administrators each control the domain (EA the whole forest). Nesting hides membership, and every machine an admin signs in to becomes a place to steal that admin. Keep these groups nearly empty and audit them recursively.

blocks.question: Which statement about Enterprise Admins is correct by default?
options: It exists in every domain
It is a member of the built-in Administrators group in every domain of the forest
It has no rights outside the schema
It is the same group as Domain Admins with a different name
blocks.explain: Enterprise Admins lives in the forest root and is nested into each domain's Administrators group, which is why compromising it gives every domain.

blocks.question: An attacker adds a permission to the AdminSDHolder object granting their account full control. What happens within about an hour?
options: Nothing, AdminSDHolder is only a template for new domains
The DC deletes the attacker's account
Windows Defender blocks the change
SDProp copies the AdminSDHolder permissions onto protected accounts and groups, so the attacker gains control of them
blocks.explain: SDProp resets protected objects to the AdminSDHolder template every 60 minutes by default. A planted entry is copied to every admin account and group, which makes AdminSDHolder a persistence target to monitor.

lessons.title: NTLM: challenge and response, and why the hash is enough

blocks.md:
Recall from the privilege escalation course (lesson 9): **NTLM** (NT LAN Manager: the authentication family from Windows NT, grown out of the older LAN Manager product) is a **challenge-response** protocol. The server sends a random number, the client proves it knows a secret by transforming that number with the secret, and the secret itself never crosses the wire. Kerberos is preferred in a domain, but Windows still falls back to NTLM, for example when you connect to a share by IP address instead of by name, or in workgroups.

Tiny example: Ana opens `\\10.0.0.20\finance` (an IP address, so no Kerberos). The file server says "prove it: here is 1122334455667788". Ana's PC answers with a 16-byte proof (plus a client blob) computed from Ana's password hash. The file server cannot check the answer itself, so it asks a DC.

blocks.title: NTLM with a domain account: three messages plus a DC check

scenes.caption: The client opens with NEGOTIATE, listing the features it supports. No secret yet.
The server answers with an 8-byte random server challenge. Fresh randomness is what stops an old answer being replayed.
The client computes the response from the challenge and the NT hash of Ana's password, which LSASS keeps after sign-in, and sends it with the user name.
The server passes the three items to a DC (pass-through authentication). The DC recomputes from its stored hash, compares, and logs event 4776.

blocks.md:
The secret both sides use is the **NT hash**: MD4 of the password encoded in UTF-16 (the MS-NLMP specification writes it `MD4(UNICODE(Passwd))`). It has **no salt**, so the same password gives the same hash on every account (recall salts from the authentication course).

- **NTLMv1** splits the NT hash into three DES keys and DES-encrypts the 8-byte challenge with each. DES (the Data Encryption Standard) has 56-bit keys and is long broken, so v1 is far weaker. Microsoft deprecated every NTLM version in June 2024 and removed NTLMv1 from Windows 11 version 24H2 and Windows Server 2025.
- **NTLMv2** first derives a per-user key, `NTOWFv2 = HMAC_MD5(NT hash, uppercase(user) + domain)`, then computes `HMAC_MD5(key, server challenge + client blob)`. The client blob adds a client challenge and a timestamp. HMAC (keyed hash, recall the crypto course) makes the response depend on the whole message.

Both share one property that matters more than the maths: **the only secret input is the stored hash**. The password is never needed.

blocks.code:
import hmac, hashlib

def ntowf_v2(nt_hash, user, domain):
    # MS-NLMP: NTOWFv2 = HMAC_MD5(NT hash, UNICODE(Uppercase(User) + UserDom))
    data = (user.upper() + domain).encode("utf-16-le")
    return hmac.new(nt_hash, data, hashlib.md5).digest()

def nt_proof(nt_hash, user, domain, server_challenge, blob):
    key = ntowf_v2(nt_hash, user, domain)
    return hmac.new(key, server_challenge + blob, hashlib.md5).digest()

# The DC stores Ana's NT hash, not the password (made-up example value)
stored_nt_hash = bytes.fromhex("0f1e2d3c4b5a69788796a5b4c3d2e1f0")
challenge = bytes.fromhex("1122334455667788")   # 8 random bytes from the server
blob = bytes.fromhex("0101000000000000aabbccddeeff0011")  # simplified client blob

# Client side: computed from the hash LSASS keeps for Ana
response = nt_proof(stored_nt_hash, "ana", "CONTOSO", challenge, blob)
# DC side: recomputes from its own copy and compares
expected = nt_proof(stored_nt_hash, "ana", "CONTOSO", challenge, blob)
print("response :", response.hex()[:16], "...")
print("match    :", hmac.compare_digest(response, expected))
# A new challenge gives a different response, so an old one cannot be replayed
other = nt_proof(stored_nt_hash, "ana", "CONTOSO", bytes.fromhex("8877665544332211"), blob)
print("new chal :", other.hex()[:16], "...")
# output:
# response : 8430bd811dbefb61 ...
# match    : True
# new chal : 1309dd5703bd0029 ...
blocks.caption: The NTLMv2 verification step from MS-NLMP, runnable with the Python standard library. The real blob also carries a timestamp and the server's name.

blocks.title: Where the password is (not) used
blocks.code:
stored = NT hash of Ana's password
challenge = server picks 8 random bytes
key = HMAC_MD5(stored, "ANA" + "CONTOSO")
response = HMAC_MD5(key, challenge + blob)
DC: expected = same steps from its copy
DC: response == expected ? allow : deny

scenes.caption: Everything starts from the stored NT hash. The DC has it in ntds.dit; Ana's PC has it in LSASS after sign-in.
The only fresh input comes from the server. It makes each response single-use.
NTLMv2 mixes in the user and domain names. Still derived only from the hash.
The response. Anyone holding the hash can compute this for any challenge: that is pass the hash.
The DC recomputes and compares. It cannot tell whether the client typed a password or replayed a stolen hash.

blocks.md:
**Defender view.**
- *Why it matters*: a stolen NT hash works as a password (pass the hash, covered from the defender's side in the privilege escalation course, lesson 9), and NTLMv1 responses captured on the network can be reversed to the hash.
- *Prevent*: set **Network security: LAN Manager authentication level** to send NTLMv2 only and refuse LM and NTLM (v1); prefer Kerberos by connecting with names, not IP addresses; put admins in **Protected Users**, which stops NTLM for them (lesson 14); and work toward restricting NTLM with the built-in NTLM auditing and blocking policies (Microsoft plans to disable network NTLM by default in a future Windows Server release).
- *Detect*: DCs log **4776** for every NTLM credential validation of a domain account, with the source workstation; failures carry codes such as `0xC000006A` (bad password). On the target, **4624** shows the authentication package, and for NTLM the package name `NTLM V1` or `NTLM V2`. Hunt for NTLM V1 at all, and for NTLM logons by admin accounts.

blocks.caption: Read-only. Microsoft's NTLMv1 audit guidance uses 4624 events with Package Name NTLM V1 to find what still depends on it.

blocks.md: NTLM never sends the password, but its proof is computed only from the unsalted NT hash plus a server challenge. So the hash is the password. Move to NTLMv2 only, then to Kerberos, and watch 4776 and the 4624 package name.

blocks.question: Why does a fresh 8-byte server challenge NOT protect against pass the hash?
options: Because the challenge is sent in plaintext
Because the attacker who holds the NT hash can compute a valid response to any new challenge
Because 8 bytes is too short
Because the DC ignores the challenge
blocks.explain: The challenge stops replay of an old response. It does nothing against someone who has the hash itself, because the hash is the only secret input.

blocks.question: An NTLM sign-in by a domain account to a file server is logged where?
options: 4776 on the DC that validated the credentials, and 4624 on the file server
Only on the client
Only in the file server's System log
Nowhere; NTLM is not audited
blocks.explain: The DC is authoritative for domain accounts and logs 4776 with the source workstation. The file server logs the resulting logon as 4624, which names the NTLM package used.

lessons.title: NTLM relay: forwarding someone else's login, and how signing stops it

blocks.md:
NTLM proves "the person at the other end knows the hash", but nothing in the basic exchange proves **which server** the client meant to talk to. A machine in the middle can therefore pass the messages along: it receives the server's challenge, hands it to the victim, takes the victim's response and gives it back to the server. The server sees a valid response and logs the attacker in **as the victim**. This is **NTLM relay** (ATT&CK T1557.001 covers the common variant). The attacker never learns the hash; they borrow one live sign-in.

Tiny example: Ana mistypes a share name, `\\fileserv`. DNS has no such host, so Windows falls back to **LLMNR** (Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution) and **NBT-NS** (NetBIOS Name Service; NetBIOS is an old naming and session service for local networks that Windows still supports), which ask the whole local network "who is fileserv?". A rogue machine answers "me", and Ana's PC starts NTLM authentication with it.

blocks.title: A relay: the attacker is a middleman for one sign-in

scenes.caption: Name resolution falls back to LLMNR or NBT-NS, which anyone on the subnet can answer. The rogue host claims the name.
Ana's PC begins NTLM with the rogue host, which opens its own connection to a real server and copies the message.
The real server's challenge is handed to Ana's PC unchanged.
Ana's PC answers the challenge; the answer is forwarded. The server validates it with the DC and logs the rogue host in as Ana.
Without signing, the session is not tied to Ana's key, so the attacker can now send any request with Ana's rights.
With SMB signing required, every message must carry a signature made with a session key derived from Ana's secret. The relayer never had it, so its requests fail.

blocks.md:
**The fixes all bind the sign-in to something the middleman lacks.**
- **SMB signing**: every SMB message carries a signature (HMAC-SHA256 or AES based) keyed by the session key. Microsoft notes the signature also confirms sender and receiver and prevents relay. DCs require it by default, as does Windows 11 24H2 (Pro and up; Server 2025: outbound); set **Microsoft network server: Digitally sign communications (always)** everywhere.
- **LDAP signing and channel binding** on DCs: reject unsigned LDAP binds and require the TLS channel binding token for LDAPS, so a relayed login cannot be used to write to the directory. With LDAP diagnostic logging on, DCs log event **2889** for clients that bind without signing.
- **EPA** (Extended Protection for Authentication) for web servers: the client folds a **channel binding token** (CBT, a value tied to the TLS connection it actually opened) into its authentication. The relayer's TLS connection to the server has a different CBT, so the server refuses.
- Remove the bait: disable LLMNR and NBT-NS where they are not needed, and reduce NTLM itself.

**Real case: PetitPotam (2021).** Microsoft's advisory KB5005413 describes PetitPotam as "a classic NTLM relay attack" that can be used against domain controllers. The pattern: an attacker **coerces** a server, which Microsoft notes can be a domain controller, into authenticating to a machine the attacker controls, then relays that machine-account login to the HTTP enrollment pages of **AD CS** (Active Directory Certificate Services, lesson 12) to request a certificate in the server's name. SpecterOps, a security firm, had documented relay to those pages weeks earlier as ESC8. Microsoft's primary mitigation is to **enable EPA and require HTTPS** on Certificate Authority Web Enrollment and Certificate Enrollment Web Service, and to disable NTLM where possible.

**Detect relay**: a 4624 network logon (type 3) with NTLM whose source IP does not belong to the account's own machine (a computer account logging on from somewhere else is a strong signal), 4776 from unexpected workstations, LLMNR or NBT-NS responses from hosts that are not DNS servers, and 2889 events on DCs.

blocks.code:
# Is SMB signing required on this server and client? (read-only)
Get-SmbServerConfiguration | Select-Object RequireSecuritySignature, EncryptData
Get-SmbClientConfiguration | Select-Object RequireSecuritySignature

# Policy-backed registry values (1 = required)
Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanManServer\Parameters' -Name RequireSecuritySignature
Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanManWorkstation\Parameters' -Name RequireSecuritySignature

# On a DC: is LDAP signing required? (LDAPServerIntegrity 2 = require signing)
Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\NTDS\Parameters' -Name LDAPServerIntegrity -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
blocks.caption: Read-only checks. The two RequireSecuritySignature values are the ones behind the 'Digitally sign communications (always)' policies.

blocks.prompt: Contoso requires SMB signing everywhere but leaves the AD CS web enrollment page on plain HTTP with NTLM and no EPA. Is the network safe from relay?
blocks.reveal: No. Relay works **across protocols**: the victim's NTLM response can be forwarded into any service that accepts NTLM without binding it to the channel. SMB signing protects SMB. An HTTP endpoint without EPA, or LDAP without signing and channel binding, is still a landing spot. That is exactly the PetitPotam to AD CS path, which is why Microsoft's fix targets the web enrollment endpoints.

blocks.md: Relay borrows a live NTLM sign-in instead of stealing a hash. It is stopped by binding authentication to the session or channel: SMB signing, LDAP signing and channel binding, and EPA on HTTPS. Then remove the bait: LLMNR, NBT-NS and NTLM itself. To respond, isolate the rogue host, review what the relayed identity did on the target, and revoke any certificate issued through a relayed login.

blocks.question: Why does requiring SMB signing defeat an SMB relay even though the relayed AUTHENTICATE message was valid?
options: Signing encrypts the challenge so it cannot be copied
Signing blocks LLMNR
Messages after sign-in must be signed with a session key derived from the victim's secret, which the relayer never learns
Signing forces Kerberos for every connection
blocks.explain: The relayer can forward the authentication but cannot compute the session key. Without it, it cannot produce valid signatures on the requests it wants to send.

blocks.question: Which control is Microsoft's primary mitigation for PetitPotam-style relay to AD CS web enrollment?
options: Disable Kerberos on the CA
Add the CA to Protected Users
Rotate the krbtgt password
Enable EPA and require HTTPS on the enrollment services
blocks.explain: KB5005413 recommends enabling Extended Protection for Authentication and disabling HTTP on the AD CS web enrollment services, so a relayed login fails the channel binding check.

lessons.title: Kerberos from zero: KDC, tickets, krbtgt and the PAC

blocks.md:
**Kerberos** is the default sign-in protocol in a domain. RFC 4120, the standard for version 5, says the name is adopted from the three-headed dog that guards Hades in Greek myth; the protocol has three parties: the **client**, the **service** and the **KDC** (Key Distribution Center) that both trust. In AD the KDC runs on every DC and uses the directory as its account database.

The core idea: instead of the password travelling to every server, the KDC hands out **tickets**, small encrypted packages that say "this is Ana, valid until 18:00", locked so that only the intended receiver can open them. Every account has a long-term **key** derived from its password, and the KDC knows all of them.

Tiny example: Ana signs in at 08:00 and opens the finance share, the intranet and SQL reports by 08:10. Ana typed the password once. Everything else used tickets.

Two exchanges, then the visit:
- **AS exchange** (Authentication Service): Ana's PC sends **AS-REQ** with **pre-authentication**, a timestamp encrypted with Ana's key, proving Ana knows the password. The KDC answers **AS-REP** with a **TGT** (ticket-granting ticket) and a session key.
- **TGS exchange** (Ticket-Granting Service): to reach a service, the PC sends **TGS-REQ** with the TGT and the service's **SPN** (Service Principal Name, the name a client uses for one instance of a service, such as `MSSQLSvc/sql01.contoso.com:1433`). The KDC answers **TGS-REP** with a **service ticket** for that SPN.
- **AP exchange** (application): the PC presents the service ticket in **AP-REQ** to the server.

The keys are the whole story. The TGT is encrypted with the key of **krbtgt**, the KDC's own account (RFC 4120 reserves the name krbtgt for the ticket-granting service). A service ticket is encrypted with the key of the **account that owns the SPN**.

blocks.title: One sign-in and one service visit, message by message

add.label: AS-REQ: ts enc. with Ana key

scenes.caption: Pre-authentication: Ana's PC encrypts the current time with the key derived from Ana's password. Only someone who knows the password can do this.
The KDC decrypts the timestamp, checks it is within the allowed clock skew (typically 5 minutes), and returns a TGT locked with the krbtgt key, plus a session key locked with Ana's key. DC logs 4768.
To reach SQL01, the PC presents the TGT and names the SPN. It does not need Ana's password again.
The KDC opens the TGT with the krbtgt key, finds who owns the SPN, and returns a service ticket locked with that account's key. DC logs 4769.
SQL01 opens the ticket with its own key, reads who Ana is and Ana's groups, and lets Ana in. It did not have to call the DC.

blocks.title: Which key locks which piece

scenes.caption: Five pieces, and the key behind each. The pre-auth timestamp (PA-TS) and the AS-REP session key are locked with Ana's key, which comes from Ana's password.
Every TGT in the domain is locked with one key: krbtgt's. Whoever has that key can mint TGTs for anyone (golden ticket, lesson 9).
A service ticket is locked with the key of the account that owns the SPN. If that account is a user with a weak password, the ticket can be cracked offline (Kerberoasting, next lesson).

Inside tickets sits the PAC, carrying the user's SIDs and groups. It has a server signature plus signatures made with the krbtgt key, so a holder of the service key alone cannot forge a fully valid PAC.

blocks.md:
**The PAC** (Privilege Attribute Certificate, Microsoft's extension defined in MS-PAC) is the authorization part of a Windows ticket: the user's SID, group memberships and related data. The KDC signs it: a **server signature** with the service's key and a **KDC signature** with the krbtgt key, which only the KDC has. Since the 2020 to 2023 hardening updates the KDC also adds a ticket signature and a signature over the full PAC, both with the krbtgt key. A server normally trusts the PAC it can verify with its own key and only goes back to a DC when it needs to validate the KDC signature. Keep this in mind for silver tickets.

**What the DC logs.** On DCs, **Audit Kerberos Authentication Service** produces **4768** (TGT requested, with the pre-authentication type and encryption type) and **4771** (pre-authentication failed; failure code `0x18` means wrong password). **Audit Kerberos Service Ticket Operations** produces **4769** (service ticket requested, with the service name and the ticket encryption type). These three event IDs carry most Kerberos detections in this course.

blocks.code:

blocks.md: Kerberos runs on keys derived from passwords. The TGT is locked with krbtgt's key; each service ticket is locked with the key of the account owning the SPN; the PAC inside carries groups and two signatures. Nearly every Kerberos attack is 'get one of those keys' or 'abuse who may ask for which ticket'.

blocks.question: SQL01 receives Ana's service ticket. What does it need to read who Ana is?
options: Its own long-term key, because the ticket was encrypted with the SQL service account's key
A live call to the DC for every connection
Ana's password
The krbtgt key
blocks.explain: The KDC encrypted the ticket with the key of the account that owns the SPN, so SQL01 decrypts it locally. That is Kerberos' efficiency gain over NTLM pass-through, and the reason a stolen service key is so powerful.

blocks.question: A DC shows a burst of 4771 events with failure code 0x18 for many different users from one IP. What is the most likely reading?
options: Clock skew on the DC
Users whose tickets expired normally
Password guessing over Kerberos: wrong passwords in pre-authentication
A replication error
blocks.explain: 4771 means pre-authentication failed and 0x18 is KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED, the wrong password. Many users from one source is the shape of password spraying (lesson 7).

lessons.title: Kerberoasting: service tickets that can be cracked offline

blocks.md:
Recall from the last lesson: a service ticket is locked with the key of the account that owns the SPN, and that key comes from the account's password. Now add one design fact: **any authenticated user may request a service ticket for any SPN**. The KDC's job is to say who you are; whether you may actually use SQL is the SQL server's decision, made later.

Put together, that is **Kerberoasting** (ATT&CK T1558.003): ask the KDC for tickets for SPNs owned by **user** accounts, carry the tickets away, and guess passwords against them **offline**. Each guess is tested by trying to decrypt the ticket; no traffic reaches the DC, so lockout never triggers and nothing is logged per guess. ATT&CK's references credit the security researcher Tim Medin with presenting it in 2014, in a talk titled "Attacking Kerberos - Kicking the Guard Dog of Hades".

Tiny example: `svc_sql` runs SQL Server and owns `MSSQLSvc/sql01.contoso.com:1433`. Its password, `Summer2019!`, was set by hand seven years ago and never changed. Any of Contoso's 3,000 users can get a ticket encrypted with that password's key.

blocks.title: Kerberoasting from the defender's seat

add.label: LDAP: users that have an SPN?

scenes.caption: Step 1 is ordinary reconnaissance: an LDAP query for user accounts with a servicePrincipalName. Any user can run it.
A normal TGS request. The KDC issues the ticket and logs 4769. If svc_sql still allows RC4, the ticket encryption type is 0x17.
The ticket leaves the network. From here on, the DC sees nothing.
Guessing is offline: derive a key from each candidate password and try to decrypt. A weak or old password falls; a long random one does not.

blocks.md:
**Why RC4 makes it worse.** For the RC4-HMAC encryption type, the Kerberos key *is* the NT hash: RFC 4757 defines it as `MD4(UNICODE(password))`, one fast unsalted hash per guess, the same value NTLM uses. For AES types, RFC 3962 derives the key with PBKDF2 (recall slow password hashing from the crypto course) using a salt and, by default, 4,096 iterations, so each guess costs thousands of hash operations. AES slows cracking a lot; it does **not** rescue `Summer2019!`, because wordlists try such passwords first.

Microsoft's own RC4 remediation guide says the RC4 default "can be abused to carry out ... Kerberoasting", changed the default for accounts without an explicit setting to AES in November 2022. Since April 2026 (KB5073381) DCs assume AES only unless an administrator explicitly allows RC4.

**Real case: Conti.** CISA, FBI and NSA's Conti advisory (AA21-265A) reports that Conti ransomware actors "use Kerberos attacks to attempt to get the Admin hash", mapped to Kerberoasting, alongside Mimikatz for credential theft.

blocks.title: Exhausting every password: length versus guessing speed

scenes.caption: Illustrative model: an offline rig testing 10 billion guesses per second (an assumption, not a benchmark). 8 random printable characters fall in about 8 days (y = -1.7); 12 take about 1.7 million years.
Drag the rate down 1,000 times, the kind of gap a slow salted key derivation creates. 8 random characters now take about 21 years. Slower hashing buys time, length buys far more.
Even at 100 trillion guesses per second, 25 random characters stay out of reach (about 10^28 years). Real human passwords are not random, so wordlists beat these curves badly.

blocks.md:
**Defender view.**
- *Prevent*: run services as **gMSAs** (group Managed Service Accounts: Windows generates the password and changes it automatically, every 30 days by default, so there is nothing human to guess). Where a user account must own an SPN, give it a long random password (ATT&CK suggests 25+ characters) and rotate it. Allow **AES only** for service accounts. Keep service accounts out of Domain Admins and other privileged groups. Delete SPNs nobody uses.
- *Detect*: on DCs, **4769** where the ticket encryption type is **0x17** for a service whose name does not end in `$` (computer accounts have random, auto-rotated passwords), in a domain that otherwise uses 0x11 and 0x12; one account requesting tickets for many different SPNs in a short window; requests for SPNs nobody normally uses.
- *Respond*: reset the targeted service account's password (or move it to a gMSA), then hunt for that account signing in from new places.

blocks.code:
# User accounts that own an SPN: each one is a Kerberoasting target.
Get-ADUser -LDAPFilter '(&(servicePrincipalName=*)(!(sAMAccountName=krbtgt)))' -Properties servicePrincipalName, pwdLastSet, 'msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes', memberOf |
  Select-Object SamAccountName,
    @{n='PasswordSet'; e={[datetime]::FromFileTime($_.pwdLastSet)}},
    @{n='EncTypes'; e={$_.'msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes'}},
    @{n='Groups'; e={$_.memberOf.Count}},
    @{n='SPNs'; e={$_.servicePrincipalName -join '; '}} |
  Sort-Object PasswordSet

# On a DC: RC4 service tickets in the last 500 4769 events, grouped by requester
Get-WinEvent -LogName Security -FilterXPath "*[System[EventID=4769] and EventData[Data[@Name='TicketEncryptionType']='0x17']]" -MaxEvents 500 |
  ForEach-Object {
    $d = @{}; ([xml]$_.ToXml()).Event.EventData.Data | ForEach-Object { $d[$_.Name] = $_.'#text' }
    [pscustomobject]@{ Requester = $d.TargetUserName; Service = $d.ServiceName }
  } | Where-Object { $_.Service -notlike '*$' } |
  Group-Object Requester | Sort-Object Count -Descending | Select-Object Count, Name
blocks.caption: Read-only. Old PasswordSet dates and EncTypes that still allow RC4 mark the accounts to fix first.

  whose account is not a computer account. In an AES-only domain this is
